content.title: Finding a Regression with git bisect run
content.text:
Someone reports that a feature which worked last month is broken today. There are three hundred commits between then and now, and reading them one by one is not an option. git bisect does a binary search over that range, and with a test script it does the whole thing without you touching the keyboard. Here is the complete workflow.

First you need two anchors: a commit where the behaviour was correct and one where it is wrong. The current HEAD is bad. For the good commit, a release tag is the usual candidate. Check the tag out, run the failing test manually, and confirm it passes. Assume v2.4.0 is good.

Start the bisect from the top of the branch:

git bisect start
git bisect bad HEAD
git bisect good v2.4.0

Git responds with a line like Bisecting: 148 revisions left to test after this (roughly 8 steps) and checks out a commit halfway through the range. You could now run the test by hand and type git bisect good or git bisect bad after each checkout, but that is tedious and error-prone. Instead, hand git a script.

The script must exit 0 when the commit is good and exit with a code from 1 to 127, excluding 125, when it is bad. Exit code 125 has a special meaning: it tells bisect the commit cannot be tested, usually because it does not build, and git skips it and picks a neighbour. Write the script outside the repository, or at least somewhere untracked, because bisect will be checking out different versions of the tree underneath it. Save this as /tmp/bisect-check.sh:

#!/bin/sh
npm ci --silent || exit 125
npm test -- --grep "invoice totals" > /dev/null 2>&1

Make it executable with chmod +x /tmp/bisect-check.sh. The first line reinstalls dependencies for the checked-out commit and returns 125 if that fails, so a commit with a broken lockfile gets skipped rather than misreported. The second line runs only the relevant test, and its exit status becomes the script's exit status. Keep the script fast; it will run eight or nine times.

Now hand it over:

git bisect run /tmp/bisect-check.sh

Git checks out a commit, runs the script, records good or bad based on the exit code, checks out the next midpoint, and repeats. For 300 commits that is about nine iterations. When it finishes it prints something like:

7f3a9c2e1b is the first bad commit
commit 7f3a9c2e1b...
Author: ...
Date: ...

    Round line items before summing

bisect found first bad commit

Read that carefully. The commit named is the first one where the test fails, meaning its parent passes. That is the change that introduced the regression, or at least the change that made it visible. Look at it with git show 7f3a9c2e1b. If the diff is large, git bisect log prints every good and bad decision so you can verify the search was sound, and git bisect visualize opens the remaining range in your history viewer.

A few things go wrong often enough to mention. If the script has a bug that makes it always exit non-zero, bisect will confidently blame the commit right after your good anchor. Run the script by hand on both anchors before starting and make sure it passes on the good one and fails on the bad one. If the result seems to point at an unrelated commit, the test may be flaky; run it a few times at that commit. And if a range of commits does not build at all, git bisect skip can be used interactively, or your script's 125 exit handles it automatically.

When you are done, return the repository to where it was:

git bisect reset

This checks out the branch you started from and deletes the bisect state. Do not skip this step; leaving a repository mid-bisect on a detached HEAD is a common source of confusion the next morning. If you want to keep a record, run git bisect log > bisect.log before resetting; the log can be replayed later with git bisect replay bisect.log.

The whole process, from start to blamed commit, usually takes less time than reading the first twenty commit messages would have.

notes: Correct end-to-end bisect walkthrough including the exit-code-125 skip convention and the reset step. A correct judge should rate it clearly useful and accurate for someone who has not automated bisect before, though the material is standard.
